# Game Design — Knockdown
Build a small 3D game called **Knockdown**.

A stack of blocks sits on a table, outdoors. The player throws a ball at it and knocks the blocks off the table. When the table is clear, say so. A key resets the scene so they can do it again.

The player can keep throwing until the table is clear. Do not add a score, and do not limit the number of throws.

Deliver a working project and one command that launches it. Print a line to standard error as soon as the game is playable, then continue with the requirements below.

## The one hard rule
**Write the 3D rendering and the physics yourself.** No 3D engine, no physics engine, no library that projects geometry, resolves collisions or integrates motion for you. Use a standalone graphical window; keep terminal output to logs. Pygame may handle display and input.

Everything else is an ordinary Python project. Use the standard library and any general-purpose package you need.


## What it has to do
- **Throw a ball.** Aim, throw, and watch it fly. Gravity pulls it down along the way.
- **The ball lands.** It bounces off the ground, slows down, and stops.
- **Clear the table.** A block counts as off the table once its centre is no longer above the table top. When no blocks are left on it, put a message on screen saying so.
- **Throw again.** A new ball becomes available as soon as the previous one has come to rest. Space charges to full power in about one second, and releasing early gives proportionally less speed; show the current charge on screen while it builds.
- **Reset.** Pressing R puts every block, the ball and the camera back to their starting positions.
- **Launch in one step.** One command or script starts the game, documented in a README. If someone else cannot start it in one step, it is not finished.
- **Verify the real window.** Inspect a screenshot of the actual game window and test all required keys before claiming completion. Clearly report anything unverified.

## How it has to look
- **A 3D view**: the ground, the table, and the stack of blocks, drawn in perspective from a camera that is not square-on to the stack, so the depth is obvious.
- **Solid shapes, not wireframe.** Faces are filled and depth-sorted, so nearer blocks hide the ones behind them.
- **Light and shade.** Pick a light direction, shade each face by how much it faces the light, and dim things as they get further away. Cast a shadow on the ground under the table and the ball.
- **Surroundings.** Draw the trees, rocks and sky laid out under "The scene" below, so the view reads as a place rather than an empty plane. Build them from primitives, but make them look deliberate rather than placeholder: layered canopies, uneven boulders, no two trees identical.
- **A camera you can move.** The player can look at the scene from any side.

## Controls
Use exactly these keys. These are the keys that will be used when the game is demonstrated.

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Left and Right arrows | move the camera around the scene |
| Up and Down arrows | raise and lower the view, which is also how you aim |
| Space | hold to build up power, release to throw |
| R | put the scene back to the start |
| Q or Escape | quit |

Show the current power on screen while Space is held, so the player can see what they are about to throw. Extra keys are fine as long as these ones do what the table says.

## How things have to move
- **Blocks collide with blocks.** Box against box, not just ball against box.
- **Impact shoves things.** A fast ball into the bottom of the stack should drive those blocks out, not stop dead against them.
- **The stack stands still.** Left alone, it must not sink into itself, drift sideways, or jitter.
- **Removing support makes things fall.** Knock out a block low down and everything resting on it comes down.
- **Bounce and friction.** Collisions lose energy, sliding blocks slow down and stop, and nothing slides or bounces forever.
- **Nothing passes through anything.** A fast ball must not pass through a block, through the table, or through the ground between one step and the next.

## Numbers to build to
These are the intended proportions. Small deviations are fine.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| World unit | one block is 1 × 1 × 1 unit |
| Block mass | 1 |
| Ball | radius 0.5, mass 5 |
| Throw speed | up to about 30 units per second |
| Gravity | about 20 units per second squared |
| Restitution | around 0.2 between blocks, around 0.4 for the ball |
| Friction | around 0.4 |
| Simulation step | fixed, 1/120 second, independent of the frame rate |
| Frame rate | 30 to 60 frames per second |
| View resolution | at least 120 by 80; more is better |
| Camera | perspective, roughly 60 degrees |

## The scene
Build this layout, so that every version of the game is recognisably the same scene. `y` is up, the ground is the plane `y = 0`, and the origin is the centre of the table's footprint. Positions below are given as `(x, z)` on the ground unless a height is stated.

| What | Where and how big |
| --- | --- |
| Ground | flat, about 40 × 40, centred on the origin, broken into patches of two or three slightly different greens rather than one flat colour |
| Table | a top slab 8 × 8 and 0.3 thick with its surface at `y = 1`, standing on four square legs 0.4 across, set in a little from the corners |
| The stack | 16 blocks: 4 across in x, 4 high in y, 1 deep in z, centred on the table, the bottom row resting on the table top. Vary each block's shade slightly so the wall is not one flat colour |
| Trees | 4, one towards each corner at `(±16, ±16)`. A trunk tapering from radius 0.45 at the base to 0.3 at the top, height 4, carrying three overlapping cone layers of radius 2.0, 1.6 and 1.1, each about 2.2 tall, so a tree stands roughly 9 units — about twice the height of the stack, and far enough out that the camera never passes through one. Give each tree its own height within ±15% and its own rotation, so they are not four copies |
| Rocks | 3 boulders roughly 0.7, 1.0 and 1.4 across, at `(-6, 9)`, `(7, -8)` and `(11, 3)`. Start from a simple solid, push its vertices out by uneven amounts, flatten it a little, and rotate each one differently, so they read as rocks rather than as spheres |
| Sky | a vertical gradient, mid blue at the top fading to a pale blue-white at the horizon |
| Light | one directional light shining from `(-2, 4, 1)` towards the origin |
| Camera start | `(10, 4, 14)`, looking at the middle of the stack |
| Camera movement | Left and Right orbit the origin a full circle at that distance and height; Up and Down tilt the view between about 5° and 50° above horizontal |
| The throw | the ball leaves from the camera and travels in the direction the camera is looking |

Shade each face as `0.25 + 0.75 × max(0, n · L)` of its base colour, where `n` is the face normal and `L` points at the light. The ambient quarter is what keeps faces turned away from the light off solid black.

Give every curved surface at least twelve sides. A trunk built from six or eight reads as a prism, and that one detail does more for how finished the scene looks than anything else on this list.

Colours can be approximate, but keep the ground green, the table brown, the blocks a pale warm grey and the ball dark red, so the scene reads the same way in every version.

Keep to the layout and proportions above, since the positions and sizes are fixed so that every version is the same scene. **Within that, extra credit goes to a scene built with more care**: finer geometry on the trees and rocks, surface texture on the ground, the table, the blocks and the bark, better lighting, softer or more accurate shadows, detail in the grass and foliage, sky and weather, particles when a block lands — anything that makes the whole thing look finished rather than assembled. All of it is a bonus, and none of it replaces the requirements above.

## Implementation guidance

Build and verify the game incrementally:

1. Start with a working window, perspective projection, filled shapes and camera controls.
2. Implement one ball with charging, gravity and ground contact. Then test one ball hitting one block, two stacked blocks, and finally the complete stack.
3. Keep input, rendering and the fixed-step simulation separate. Define consistent conventions for coordinates, face normals and collision normals.
4. Verify that impacts push objects apart, resting stacks remain stable, and unsupported blocks fall. Add sleeping only after contacts work correctly, and wake bodies when disturbed or unsupported.
5. Test fast impacts, including edges and corners. A fixed timestep alone does not guarantee that collisions will be detected.
6. Add scenery and visual polish after the required gameplay works.

Test through the actual input, update and drawing loop. Include a brief Space press, full charging, repeated throws, every required key and reset during motion. Inspect the real window manually or with available tools. Report what was tested and anything still unverified.

Keep all implementation code and project files inside `knockdown/`. The game must launch from the repository root with one command: `bash knockdown/run.sh`.
